judge_assessment.explanation: The judge's mathematics and its praise for the quadrant treatment both hold up. I converted every point independently: (6, pi/3) to (3, 3 sqrt 3); (3, 4) to (5, 53.13 deg); (4, 3pi/4) to (-2 sqrt 2, 2 sqrt 2); (-2, 2) to (2 sqrt 2, 135 deg) with 315 correctly rejected as the opposite ray through (2, -2); tan theta = sqrt 3 with r = 4 in quadrant III giving (-2, -2 sqrt 3); (6, 210 deg) to (-3 sqrt 3, -3); (-3, -4) to (5, 233.13 deg); (-4, 4) to (4 sqrt 2, 135 deg); r = 4 cos theta at pi/3 giving (1, 1.73) and, multiplied through by r, x^2 + y^2 = 4x, i.e. (x-2)^2 + y^2 = 4, a circle of radius 2 centred at (2, 0) — all correct. I also checked the standards tags against references/standards-map.md line 118, 'Parametric & polar representations | HSF-IF.C.7, HSN-CN.B.4-B.6', and the key reproduces that row exactly rather than substituting a lower-grade code. I checked the pages for text collisions with pdftotext -bbox and rendered the one candidate it reported (page 3, a radical against the word 'point'); the rendered page is clean, so that is a poppler boxing artifact and the visual score of 4 is deserved. Where I part from the perfect 32 is the open-response accounting. The package declares two manual items (9b and 10c) and final_response.md says so explicitly, but four more problems print a request whose answer is a sentence and none of them is declared: problem 2 asks 'Which quadrant is the point in, and does the arctangent key need any correction here?'; problem 4(c) asks 'Say which of the two is the polar angle of this point, and why the other one is wrong'; problem 7 asks 'Compare your work with problem 2 ... what exactly is different about the answer?'; problem 8(c) asks for the correct theta 'explaining the adjustment you had to make'. The key answers all four in prose. Separately, problem 8(b) instructs the student to 'Type y/x into your calculator's arctangent key and write down what it returns' — the requested answer is -45 — and that value appears nowhere in verify.json or in the Quick Answers row ('8. 4 sqrt 2, 135'). Worse, the key's front-page 'Common wrong answers' block reads '8. If they got -45: typed the ratio into the arctangent key and wrote down whatever appeared', so a teacher grading 8(b) from that block would mark a correct response as the misconception. The worked solution handles it properly ('the arctangent key returns -45 ... the key always answers in (-90, 90)'), but the fast-grading surface does not.

strengths_to_preserve: The sheet's thesis is stated in the directions and then enforced by the problem design: 'tan theta = y/x has two solutions on [0, 360), half a turn apart, and the arctangent key only ever returns one of them. Plot the point, see the quadrant, and pick the solution that lands there.' Problems 4, 5 and 10 then require the student to solve for BOTH candidates explicitly and choose, rather than being handed a single arctangent value.

Problems 2 and 7 are a deliberately matched pair: (3, 4) and (-3, -4) share the 3-4-5 triangle and the same tangent ratio because the two minus signs cancel, and problem 7 asks the student to say what differs. The key closes it precisely — 'The tangent alone cannot tell these two points apart — which is why the plot is not optional.' That is the cleanest possible demonstration of why the quadrant decision exists.

Problem 8 makes the calculator itself the object of study rather than a black box: part (b) has the student type the ratio in and record -45, and the key explains the structural reason — 'The key always answers in (-90, 90) — quadrants I and IV only — so it can never return a quadrant II angle no matter what is typed in.' Explaining the arctangent's range is exactly the right level of explanation for a precalculus student.

Problem 10 covers the degenerate case the formula cannot reach: x = 0 on the y-axis, where tan theta = y/x is undefined, solved instead through cos theta = 0 with the sign of y choosing between 90 and 270. Including the case where the taught formula fails, and declaring the explanation manual, is what makes the treatment complete rather than merely procedural.

Problem 9's key explains the derivation's non-obvious first move rather than just performing it: 'Why multiply by r first: the conversion identities are r^2 = x^2 + y^2, x = r cos theta and y = r sin theta. A bare cos theta matches none of them; r cos theta matches one exactly.' It also verifies the derived circle against the part (a) point, closing the loop between the two halves of the problem.

Every worked solution ends with a magnitude check (x^2 + y^2 = r^2) and a sign-versus-quadrant check, and problem 6's check is given in decimals — 'about (-5.20, -3), which is where the plot lands' — tying the exact answer back to the printed grid the student used.

root_causes.description: Four problems print an explanation or decision request whose answer is a sentence, and none is declared manual. The package therefore reports two open items on a sheet that prints six. The pattern is consistent: the numeric half of each problem is recorded and the reasoning half — which on a quadrant-selection worksheet is the assessed skill — is not.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 2: 'Which quadrant is the point in, and does the arctangent key need any correction here?' verify.json id 2 has an eval and an approx, no manual entry.
worksheet.pdf problem 4(c): 'Say which of the two is the polar angle of this point, and why the other one is wrong.' verify.json id 4 has an eval and a solve_interval, no manual entry.

worksheet.pdf problem 7: 'Compare your work with problem 2: the two points use the same right triangle, so what exactly is different about the answer?' verify.json id 7 has an eval and an approx, no manual entry.
worksheet.pdf problem 8(c): '... give the correct theta in degrees, explaining the adjustment you had to make.' verify.json id 8 has an eval and an approx, no manual entry.
verify.json ids 9 and 10 DO carry manual entries, and final_response.md states 'Flagged for manual review (2 items)', so the mechanism was in use and simply not applied consistently.

root_causes.description: Several printed answer slots have no declared expected value, so they cannot reach the Quick Answers bank. Problem 8(b) explicitly asks the student to record the calculator's arctangent output (-45) and no entry covers it. Problem 2's quadrant answer and its yes/no correction answer are uncovered. Problem 4(c)'s chosen angle is not distinguished from the two candidates, so the bank's '2 sqrt 2, 135, 315' leaves the actual answer ambiguous. And problem 9(b)'s derived rectangular equation (x-2)^2 + y^2 = 4 is a machine-checkable result declared wholly manual, so the correct curve equation never reaches the bank even though only the derivation needs a human.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 8(b): 'Type y/x into your calculator's arctangent key and write down what it returns.' No verify entry has expected -45; answer_key.pdf bank row is '8. 4 sqrt 2, 135'.
answer_key.pdf bank row '4. 2 sqrt 2, 135, 315' against worksheet.pdf problem 4(c), which asks which of the two is the polar angle — the row lists both without marking the answer.

verify.json id 9's manual entry covers the whole of part (b) including the naming of the curve; answer_key.pdf gives the equation (x-2)^2 + y^2 = 4 and the name 'circle of radius 2 centred at (2, 0)', neither of which is in the bank row '9. 1, 1.73'.
worksheet.pdf problem 2 asks for the quadrant and whether a correction is needed; the bank prints '2. 5, 53.13'.

root_causes.description: The key's front-page 'Common wrong answers' block flags -45 as a misconception for problem 8, but problem 8(b) instructs the student to produce exactly that value and write it down. The worked solution disambiguates (it is wrong only if reported as the final theta), but the standalone block does not carry that qualification, so the grading aid contradicts the printed instruction.
evidence: answer_key.pdf 'Common wrong answers': '8. If they got -45: typed the ratio into the arctangent key and wrote down whatever appeared'.
worksheet.pdf problem 8(b): 'Type y/x into your calculator's arctangent key and write down what it returns.'

answer_key.pdf worked solution 8 Step 2 states the correct nuance — the key returns -45 and always answers in (-90, 90) — and its in-solution note says '-45: the key's output was copied without adjusting for the quadrant', which is the missing qualification.

root_causes.description: Problems 9 and 10 mix machine entries with declared manual entries and their bank rows show no manual marker, because render_entry reaches the em-dash fallback only when a problem has no machine-expected values at all. The two items the author correctly flagged are invisible in the column a teacher grades from.
evidence: verify.json id 9: two approx entries plus one manual entry; answer_key.pdf bank row '9. 1, 1.73'.
verify.json id 10: three machine entries plus one manual entry; bank row '10. 5, 90, 270, -5'.
scripts/render_quick_answers.py render_entry: the '---' fallback is guarded by 'if not vals'.

improvements.title: Declare the quadrant-decision explanations in problems 2, 4(c), 7 and 8(c) as manual items
improvements.proposed_change: Require a manual verify entry for every printed request whose answer is a sentence, including when it hangs off a computed part of the same problem. Enforce with a lint over the worksheet source that matches decision and explanation imperatives ('say which ... and why', 'explaining the adjustment', 'what exactly is different', 'does ... need any correction') and fails when the corresponding verify id lacks a manual entry. Also settle in SKILL.md whether a per-problem plotting grid implies a graded drawn response: every problem here supplies a polar grid and says 'Plot it', and the directions treat the plot as a method step, but problem 8(c) reads as though the plot is part of the answer. Either the grids are scaffolding and SKILL.md should say so, or a supplied grid should force a manual entry.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture from curr-431 problem 4: prompt part (c) 'Say which of the two is the polar angle of this point, and why the other one is wrong', with a verify id containing only an eval and a solve_interval. The gate must exit non-zero naming the unflagged decision, and pass once a manual entry is added. Assert that a full curr-431-shaped fixture's declared manual count rises from 2 to 6.
improvements.expected_impact: Triples the honestly declared open surface on a sheet whose whole thesis is that the quadrant decision is reasoning a calculator cannot do. Makes final_response.md's 'Flagged for manual review (2 items)' accurate rather than an undercount.
improvements.risk: Text scanning over-triggers on instructional asides and under-triggers on requests phrased as questions; needs an author override and calibration against baseline worksheets before it hard-fails. Forcing a manual entry for every supplied grid would also inflate manual counts on sheets where plotting is genuinely only a working step.

improvements.title: Cover the requested calculator output, the quadrant answer, the chosen angle and the derived curve equation
improvements.proposed_change: Enforce a response-slot inventory built from the worksheet source so every printed request binds to a declared expected value or a manual entry. Three specific consequences here: (i) problem 8(b)'s requested calculator output -45 becomes a declared approx entry rather than existing only in the key's prose; (ii) problem 4(c)'s chosen angle is declared separately from the candidate list so the bank can print 'candidates 135, 315; answer 135' instead of an ambiguous triple; (iii) where a manual entry covers a derivation whose RESULT is machine-checkable — problem 9(b)'s (x-2)^2 + y^2 = 4 — require an accompanying equiv entry so the derivation stays manual while the result reaches the bank.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture from curr-431 problem 8: a three-part prompt whose part (b) asks for the arctangent key's output, with verify.json declaring only r and the corrected angle. The gate must fail naming the uncovered slot; after adding an approx entry expected -45, the fixture passes and the bank row reads '(a) 4 sqrt 2; (b) -45; (c) 135'. Add a second case asserting that a manual entry whose model answer contains a boxed equation triggers a warning when no equiv entry accompanies it.
improvements.expected_impact: Restores four requested answers to the grading column on this sheet, including the two — the raw calculator output and the derived circle equation — that carry the most teaching weight. The manual-plus-equiv pattern generalises to every derivation item in the suite.
improvements.risk: Splitting a candidate list into 'candidates' and 'answer' changes the shape of solve_interval consumers and needs a migration; and requiring an equiv beside a manual derivation will produce false alarms on derivations whose result genuinely is prose (a named curve, a case rule).

improvements.title: Suppress or qualify a common-wrong-answer entry whose value the worksheet explicitly asks the student to record
improvements.proposed_change: Cross-check each declared trap value against the expected value of every other entry under the same problem id, and against every printed answer slot for that problem. When the same value is a legitimately requested response, either suppress the common-wrong-answers entry or emit it naming the quantity and the qualification the worked solution already carries ('If they gave -45 as the FINAL angle: ...'). Concept-model and error-analysis items that deliberately have the student reproduce a wrong-method output are a recurring design, and the trap block must not contradict the printed instruction.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture where problem 8 declares an approx entry with expected -45 for part (b) and a trap with value -45. Assert the generated common-wrong-answers block either omits the entry or renders it with the 'as the final answer' qualification, and assert the unqualified string 'If they got -45: typed the ratio into the arctangent key' is not emitted. It is emitted today.
improvements.expected_impact: Prevents a teacher grading from the key's front page from marking a correct response to problem 8(b) as the misconception it is designed to expose. Small but directly harmful when it happens, since the student did exactly what was asked.
improvements.risk: Suppressing a trap entry loses a genuinely useful grading hint for students who report the value as their final answer; the qualified-wording branch is preferable and needs the slot inventory to know which part requested the value.

improvements.title: Show a manual-review marker on Quick Answers rows that mix machine and manual entries
improvements.proposed_change: Change scripts/render_quick_answers.py render_entry so a problem whose entry list contains a type == 'manual' appends an explicit marker to its bank row, rather than reaching the manual em-dash only when the problem has no machine entries at all. Add a legend line beneath the bank.
improvements.regression_test: Render curr-431's verify.json ids 9 and 10 (each mixing machine entries with a manual entry) and assert both bank rows carry a manual marker. Both render today as bare number lists, so the assertion fails before the fix; assert a manual-only problem still renders the plain em-dash.
improvements.expected_impact: Makes the two correctly declared manual items visible where a teacher grades. On this sheet those are the curve derivation and the y-axis explanation — the two items the key spends the most space on.
improvements.risk: Extra row width reduces the adaptive column count on dense sheets; use a single glyph rather than a word.

case_summary: An excellent guided-practice packet on coordinate conversion whose organising idea is that the quadrant decision is reasoning, not calculator output. Every problem carries its own polar grid, problems 4, 5 and 10 make the student produce BOTH tangent candidates and choose, problems 2 and 7 are a matched pair on the same 3-4-5 triangle that differ only by quadrant, problem 8 makes the arctangent key's restricted range the object of study, and problem 10 covers the y-axis case where the taught formula fails. I converted every point independently and found no error; the standards tags reproduce references/standards-map.md line 118 exactly; and the one text collision my bbox scan reported turned out to be a poppler artifact — the rendered page is clean, so visual quality 4 is right. ACCEPT is correct. The gap under the perfect 32 is open-response accounting: the package declares two manual items and final_response.md says so, but problems 2, 4(c), 7 and 8(c) each print a request whose answer is a sentence and none is declared. Problem 8(b) also asks the student to record the calculator's -45 and that requested value is neither verified nor banked — while the key's front-page common-wrong-answers block flags -45 as the misconception, so a teacher grading 8(b) from that block would mark a correct answer wrong.
